title: The Neuron in the Basement
setting: a clock-repair shop with a strange machine

post.author: u/mainspring_magda
post.title: My great-uncle left me his clock-repair shop and a machine in the basement that learns. I let it learn faster, and it set a clock to a time that hasn't happened yet.

blocks.text: I repair clocks in the shop my great-uncle Anselm ran for forty years. In the basement is what he built in his last ten: a cabinet of tiny brass dials, thousands of them, each turned by its own little motor. His notebook calls it the learner.

His first lesson wires up one small rack, a back row of four brass units and one at the front, 17 dials in all, plus four punched cards. Every card shows an hour hand pointing right, where 3 sits on an ordinary clock face. One hole means it's a backwards clock, the kind barbers hang to be read in a mirror. The other means you're seeing it in a mirror. Either flip alone makes it 9 o'clock. Both together cancel out: 3 again. The rack reads each card and sets one of four little clocks on its front to its answer, in hours after midnight.

After each pass through the four cards, a lesson, every dial turns a little, and a paper tape prints the loss: square each clock's miss in hours, then average the four. Zero would be perfect. A brass knob marked STRIDE sets how far the dials turn. It has four stops, 0, 0.01, 0.1 and 1.5, and his pencil mark is at 0.1.
For three nights a rotted cable cut the back row out, and the cards went straight to the front unit: 3 dials. The loss fell to 9.00 and stopped there. All four clocks said six.

On Thursday I replaced the cable, reset the dials to the starting positions the notebook lists, random numbers in his hand, and started again at 0.1. In 300 lessons the loss went from 51.14 to 0.085. Too slow, I thought, so I turned the knob to 1.5.

Three lessons, and it was better than ever. Then the fourth clock started to swing: under 3, over, under again, further each time. At lesson 306 it read 1:09, and the tape said 25.143 hours. Not 1:09 this morning. 1:09 tomorrow, a time that hadn't happened yet.
It wasn't learning the time. It was running ahead of it.
I pulled the main switch at lesson 312. It was eight minutes to midnight. The tape's last line says 2524.54 hours, more than a hundred days ahead. I sat on the stairs until 1:09 anyway.
Why does it get worse the faster I let it learn? And what do I change before tonight?

Lesson 303: 3.15 hours, loss 0.022. Two lessons later, lesson 305: 1.27 hours, loss 3.83. Lesson 306: 25.143 hours, which is 1:09 tomorrow, loss 307.32. Lesson 307: minus 49.53 hours, loss 5245.37. Lesson 308: 163.41 hours, loss 24786.44. The misses grow every lesson.

blocks.caption: I copied the tape into boxes on Friday morning. Clock 4 should say 3 hours. At 0.1 it was 0.34 off and closing. At 1.5 it got closer for three lessons, then missed by 1.73, 22.14, 52.53 and 160.41 hours, on alternate sides, each miss bigger than the last. Lesson 306 is the one that read 1:09 tomorrow.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Glad you pulled the switch, and glad you kept the tape. Nothing in that cabinet is haunted: you have a small neural network. Each brass unit is a neuron. It multiplies each input by a dial (engineers call it a weight), adds them up, and adds one more dial (a bias). The back-row neurons then pass that total through a soft switch (an activation) that slides from off, 0, to on, 1. The front one skips the switch, so its answer can be any number of hours. Four in the back with three dials each, one in front with five: your 17. The back row is a hidden layer. Each lesson, the machine works out which way every dial should turn to lower the loss and turns them all a little that way: gradient descent. STRIDE is the learning rate, how far each turn goes, and one lesson through every card is an epoch. Two questions. In the last few lessons before you pulled the switch, how big was each lesson's biggest dial turn compared with the one before? And why did the cut-out rack stop at exactly 9.00?

replies.author: u/mainspring_magda
replies.text: The tape has a column for that I didn't post. Lessons 309 to 312: 472.23, 944.45, 1888.90, 3777.80. Each one twice the last. And 9.00 is six o'clock on every card: three hours off from both 3 and 9, and three squared is nine. It found the middle and stayed there.

comments.author: u/regulator_ilse
comments.text: Forty years regulating pendulum clocks. When one gains, you give the regulating nut a small turn, wait a day and read it again. Shove the nut and you chase the clock fast, slow, fast all week. Turn it a hair at a time and the customer is back before it keeps time. Every regulator I trained learned the size of a turn by getting it wrong both ways.

comments.author: u/night_run_ivo
comments.text: I train models for a living, and the shape of your tape gave me a chill. One of our training runs looked fine for two days, then the loss jumped, then the log said inf, infinity, a number too big for the computer to store. Then it said NaN, short for not a number, which is what you get when a sum uses infinity in a way that has no answer, like infinity minus infinity. The job didn't crash. It ran for six more hours, carefully computing nothing.

reply.prompt: Magda runs the learner again tonight. What should she change before she starts? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Leave the knob at 1.5 and let it run all night. The swings are the machine searching, and they'll settle once it finds the time.
options.part2: I left it at 1.5 and went to bed. The tape tells the rest. Every lesson, the four clocks spun longer to reach their answers. At lesson 812 the loss column printed Infinity: the number had grown too big for the machine to hold. The dials kept turning, further each lesson, until lesson 1,321, when every column printed NaN and every motor in the rack stopped at once. In the morning the four little clocks had no answer at all.
options.senior: Swings that grow every step are divergence, not searching. Each step overshoots the low point by more than the last, so more steps only make it worse. Lower the learning rate.

options.text: Reset the dials and set the knob to 0.01. Steps that small can never swing past the answer, so it can't run away from the time again.
options.verdict: Trade-off: safe, but ten times slower
options.part2: I reset the dials and set 0.01. It never swung once. It also crept: 8.82 after 100 lessons, 8.55 after 300, 5.54 after 1,000. It reached 0.078 at lesson 3,000, about where 0.1 had been at lesson 300. Same road, ten times the lessons. I opened the shop late, and the next lesson in the notebook uses thousands of dials, not 17.
options.senior: A tiny learning rate is safe here but slow: the dials walked almost the same path as at 0.1, in ten times the lessons. On a big model that is days of extra training. You usually want the largest rate whose loss still falls steadily.

options.text: Turn the knob back to 0.1 and carry on from lesson 312. The dials have already learned most of it, so there's no reason to start over.
options.part2: I turned it back to 0.1 and let it carry on. Within a hundred lessons the swings had died away, and the tape settled on a loss of 9.00. Every clock said six, exactly like the nights the cable was cut. At lesson 1,312 it was still 9.00. The rack had all 17 dials and the sense of 3 of them.
options.senior: After a blow-up the weights are so large that the switches sit fully on or off and pass back almost no blame, so a smaller step can't undo the damage. Restart from sensible dials, or from a copy saved before it went wrong.

options.text: Reset the dials, go back to 0.1 and read the tape every hundred lessons. If the loss ever starts climbing, turn the knob down, not up.
options.part2: I reset the dials, went back to 0.1 and read the tape every hundred lessons. Lesson 300: 0.085, same as Thursday. I left the knob alone. Lesson 400: 0.005. Lesson 500: 0.0003, and the four clocks read 3:01, 8:59, 8:59 and 3:01. Then I found a scrap of paper wedged behind the STRIDE knob, in Anselm's hand: a column of numbers, each twice the one above, and at the bottom, too far, back to 0.1. He'd been down those stairs too.
options.senior: When the loss explodes, lower the learning rate and restart from sensible dials, not from the wreck. Then read the loss curve: steady falls mean the step fits; swings that grow mean it's too big. Watching the curve is the whole safety system.

sim.title: Teach the rack yourself
sim.lede: You're Magda on Friday night in the basement. Top left is the rack: the two holes feed the four back-row neurons, which feed the front neuron, and every line is one weight, a dial (thicker means a bigger dial, dashed means negative). Top right are the four clocks: the solid hands are the machine's answer, the dashed hand is the right hour, and clock 4 is the backwards clock in a mirror, whose right answer is 3. The chart plots the loss after every lesson. Each gridline up is ten times the one below, because the loss can climb from under 0.01 to past 100 million. Turn the STRIDE knob (the learning rate), teach 1 or 100 lessons at a time (each lesson is one epoch), and cut the back row out to try one neuron alone. Switching the back row, or Reset, puts the dials back at Thursday's random starting positions, at lesson 0. The loss here is measured on the same four cards the rack learns from: it shows whether the rack can learn them, not how it would do on a card it has never seen.
sim.tryThis: Try this: teach 100 lessons three times at 0.1. Lesson 300: loss 0.085, clock 4 at 3.34 hours, Thursday's tape. Now turn the knob to 1.5 and teach 1 lesson at a time. Three lessons get better, then clock 4 swings: 1.27, then 25.143 (1:09 tomorrow), then -49.53, and from lesson 309 the biggest dial turn doubles every lesson. Keep teaching: the loss reads Infinity from lesson 812 and NaN at lesson 1321, where the rack stops. Reset and try 0.01: after 300 lessons the loss is still 8.55. Cut the back row out at 0.1: the loss stops at 9.00 and every clock says 6:00, however long you teach. Last, set the knob to 0 and teach: nothing moves at all.

explain.oneLine: Nothing haunted the learner. At 0.1 each lesson turned its 17 dials a little downhill and the loss fell from 51.14 to 0.085; at 1.5 every turn overshot the low point by more than the last, so the swings grew until the numbers no longer fit.

steps.title: A neuron is a weighted sum, a bias and a soft switch.
steps.text: Each brass unit in the rack is a neuron. It multiplies each input by its own weight, one dial each, adds the results, and adds one more dial, the bias. Google's Machine Learning Crash Course describes a hidden neuron the same way: the sum of each input times a unique weight, plus the bias. Then comes the activation, a soft switch. The back row uses a sigmoid, which turns any total into a number between 0 (off) and 1 (on), sliding smoothly in between. The front neuron skips the switch, so its answer can be any number of hours. Training never rewires anything. It only turns dials: 12 in the back row and 5 in front, the 17 parameters of this model.

steps.title: One neuron can't read a mirror. A layer of switches can.
steps.text: With the back row cut out, the answer was a weighted sum of the two holes plus a bias. Punching a hole adds the same amount to the answer whatever the other hole says. The mirror cards need the opposite: either hole alone adds six hours, and both together add nothing. No weighted sum can do that, and the best compromise is 6 for every card, three hours from each right answer, a loss of exactly 9. This is the classic XOR pattern: yes when exactly one of two things is true. More layers of plain weighted sums wouldn't help, because, as Google's course puts it, linear operations performed on linear operations are still linear. The switches are non-linear, and that makes the difference. Each back-row neuron can switch on for its own combination of holes, and the front neuron adds those up, so together they can make two holes cancel, which no single neuron can.

steps.title: Loss is one number, and gradient descent turns every dial a little downhill.
steps.text: The loss squeezes four misses into one number: square each clock's miss in hours and average them, which engineers call mean squared error. Google's course calls loss a numerical metric that describes how wrong a model's predictions are. For each dial, the gradient says which way the loss would move if that dial turned a hair, and how steeply. Gradient descent turns every dial a small step against its gradient, downhill, then measures again: in Google's words, move the weight and bias values a small amount in the direction that reduces loss, and repeat. 3Blue1Brown's series puts it as: compute this gradient direction, take a step downhill, and repeat that over and over. One lesson through all four cards is one epoch, and the learner takes one step per epoch. At 0.1 the loss fell in every one of the first 300 lessons: a quick drop to about 9 (8.95 at lesson 5), a slow stretch while the back row sorted itself out (8.18 at lesson 50), then down to 0.085 at lesson 300 and 0.0003 at lesson 500.

steps.title: Backpropagation passes the blame backwards.
steps.text: To turn 17 dials the right way, the learner needs each dial's share of the blame, and it gets them all in one backward sweep. Start at the clock: how far off was it, and which way? The front neuron's dials get blame in proportion to what flowed through them. The front neuron then passes blame back to each back-row neuron, scaled by the dial between them and by how responsive that neuron's switch was: a switch sitting almost fully on or off barely responds, so it passes back little blame. Each back-row neuron shares its blame among its own dials. That backward sweep is backpropagation, and it hands gradient descent every dial's gradient at once. 3Blue1Brown calls it an algorithm for computing that negative gradient, and Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams described it in Nature in 1986.

steps.title: The learning rate: too small crawls, too big swings further each time.
steps.text: Each dial's turn is its gradient times the learning rate, Anselm's STRIDE. At 0.01 the dials walked almost the same path as at 0.1 but took ten times the lessons: 0.078 at lesson 3,000. At 1.5 each turn carried the dials past the low point and up the far side, higher than where they started. There the slope was steeper, so the next turn was bigger and overshot further: a swing that grows instead of settling. From lesson 309 the biggest dial turn doubled every lesson. At lesson 812 the loss grew too big to store and read Infinity, and at lesson 1,321 a sum involving infinity gave NaN, after which nothing can be learned. Language models learn with this same loop of a loss, gradients from backpropagation and a learning rate; their loss scores how well they predicted the next word (strictly, the next token). Case 6 of this season shows it.

diagram.aria: One lesson of the learner, forward then backward. Forward: a card's 2 holes, each 0 or 1, go to the back row of 4 neurons (sum, bias and switch), whose outputs go to the front neuron (sum and bias, no switch), whose answer sets clock 4: 3.34 hours at lesson 300, right answer 3. The miss goes into the loss, one number: 0.085. Backward: the blame goes from the loss to the front neuron's dials (the miss times what came in), then back to the back row's dials (times the dial in between and the switch's slope), and then every one of the 17 dials turns a little, learning rate times blame, before the next lesson repeats it.

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right, then the bottom row right to left. Forward, the card's two holes pass through the back row's four switches and the front neuron's sum to an answer on clock 4: 3.34 hours at lesson 300. The loss turns the four misses into one number, 0.085. Backward, the blame starts at the miss, reaches the front neuron's dials, then passes to the back row, scaled by the dial in between and by how responsive each switch is. Then all 17 dials turn a little, the learning rate times their blame. Forward and backward through all four cards is one lesson: one epoch.

fix.title: The fix: a step size that fits, chosen by watching the loss
fix.text: Reset the dials first. After a blow-up they're wound so far that the back-row switches sit fully on or off and barely respond: turn the knob back to 0.1 without a reset and the rack settles at 6:00 for every card, a loss of 9.00, no better than one neuron. Then choose the learning rate by trying it. From the same starting dials, give each knob setting a short run and read the loss curve. A curve that falls steadily means the step fits. One that falls and then swings upward means the step is too big, and one that barely moves means it's too small. On this rack that's 0.1. Keep watching the curve for the whole run, and when the loss climbs, lower the rate rather than raising it to push through; Google's course notes that lowering the learning rate can help prevent exploding gradients. Google's Deep Learning Tuning Playbook goes further: different learning rates work best at different times during training, so it recommends some schedule that changes the rate as training goes on. And for a real task, keep case 1's habit: a low loss on the examples a model trains on is only half the check.

limits: Four cards only test whether the rack can learn these four. The loss here is measured on the very cards it learns from, so it says nothing about a card it has never seen. On a real task you'd also track the loss on held-back examples, as in case 1.

There's no universal right learning rate. The safe size depends on the model, the data and where the dials are, which is why it's found by trying, not looked up: 0.1 suits this rack and these four cards, and means nothing for another model.

Gradient descent only walks downhill from where it starts. It can crawl across flat stretches, like the lessons near a loss of 9 before the back row found the pattern, and on harder problems it can settle somewhere that isn't the lowest point. Different starting dials can end differently.

Aims for fast early progress and a careful finish.
Hard to blow up, but it can run out of time or crawl on flat stretches.

More settings to get wrong: when to lower the rate, and by how much.
What the loss curve looks like
A climb, or a fall followed by swings that grow.
A fast drop, then a slower, steadier finish, if the schedule fits.

explain.seniorTake: When training goes wrong, read the loss curve before touching anything else. A curve that barely moves means steps that are too small, or a model that can't draw the pattern at all, like one neuron on the mirror cards. A curve that swings wider every step means steps that are too big, and NaN is the end of that road, not a new mystery. Lower the learning rate before adding dials, restart from sensible dials rather than from the wreck, and judge the result by the curve.

realWorld.title: 3Blue1Brown's Neural networks series
realWorld.text: The series trains a network to read handwritten digits: 784 inputs, one per pixel of a 28 by 28 image, two hidden layers of 16 neurons and 10 outputs, with 13,002 weights and biases in all, against the learner's 17. Its cost function is the same idea as the learner's loss: add up the squares of the differences between what the network gave and what you want, then average over tens of thousands of training examples. When it talks about a network learning, it means changing the weights and biases to minimize a cost function, and its gradient descent is: compute this gradient direction, take a step downhill, and repeat that over and over. It adds that if your step sizes are proportional to the slope, they get smaller and smaller as the slope flattens out toward a minimum, and that keeps you from overshooting, as long as the learning rate itself is small enough, which the learner's 1.5 was not.

realWorld.title: 3Blue1Brown on backpropagation
realWorld.text: The series' backpropagation chapter calls it an algorithm for computing that negative gradient: the nudges to all 13,002 weights and biases that lower the cost most efficiently. It builds it the way the learner's back row does: the last layer's wished-for changes become nudges for the layer before, added up across neurons in proportion to the weights, and the same is repeated layer after layer, backwards. It also explains stochastic gradient descent: each step uses a mini-batch of examples instead of the whole training set, which isn't the exact downhill direction but is a pretty good approximation, and much faster.

realWorld.title: Google's Machine Learning Crash Course on the learning rate
realWorld.text: Google's course says the model multiplies the gradient by the learning rate to set its weights and bias for the next step: with a gradient of 2.5 and a learning rate of 0.01, the parameter changes by 0.025. If the learning rate is too low, the model can take a long time to converge; if it is too high, the model never converges, but instead bounces around the weights and bias that minimize the loss. It defines an epoch as the model having processed every example in the training set once, and notes that training typically requires many epochs.

realWorld.title: Back-propagation in Nature, 1986
realWorld.text: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams described back-propagation in Nature in 1986 as a learning procedure for networks of neurone-like units. It repeatedly adjusts the weights of the connections in the network to minimize a measure of the difference between the network's actual output and the desired output. As the weights adjust, they wrote, internal hidden units, which are neither input nor output, come to represent important features of the task, and that ability to create useful new features is what distinguishes back-propagation from earlier, simpler methods such as the perceptron-convergence procedure. The learner's back row is that idea at its smallest: four hidden units that learn, between them, what a mirror does to a clock.

asked: Explain how a neural network learns to a non-technical stakeholder.
What does the learning rate do, and what happens when it's too high?
interview.answer: For the stakeholder, use dials. A neural network is a set of dials between the input and the answer: a tiny one might have 17, the models behind chat assistants have billions. We show it examples with known answers and score how wrong it is with one number, the loss. Then every dial turns a little in whichever direction lowers that number. Backpropagation is the bookkeeping that works out each dial's share of the blame, working backwards from the answer. Repeat over all the examples many times and the dials settle where the answers come out right. Whether it also works on examples it never saw is a separate check we always run. The learning rate sets the size of each turn: the gradient times the rate. Too small and training crawls, burning time and money. Too high and each step overshoots the low point, so the loss bounces, or grows every step until it overflows to infinity and then NaN. I choose it with short trial runs from the same start, watch the loss curve the whole way, often lower it on a schedule as training goes on, and when a run blows up I lower the rate and restart from a saved copy of the weights from before it went wrong, not from the wreck.

terms.def: One small unit of a neural network. It multiplies each input by a weight, adds them up with a bias, and usually passes the total through an activation. Each brass unit in the learner is one.
A number inside a neuron that scales one input: how much that input counts. This case calls weights dials. Training turns them.
One more dial inside a neuron, added to the weighted sum whatever the inputs are. It shifts the neuron's answer up or down.
Each input multiplied by its weight, then all added up.
What a neuron does to its weighted sum before passing it on, usually a soft switch such as a sigmoid. Also called an activation function.
This case's plain name for an activation like the sigmoid: it slides smoothly from off (0) to on (1) instead of flipping.
An S-shaped activation, 1 / (1 + e^-x). Very negative totals give nearly 0, very positive ones nearly 1, and it slides smoothly in between.
A model made of neurons in layers, each layer's outputs feeding the next. Training turns its weights and biases. The learner's 17-dial rack is a tiny one.
A row of neurons that all read the same inputs and pass their outputs on to the next row.
A layer between the inputs and the output. The learner's back row is one.
A neuron in a hidden layer, neither an input nor an output. The 1986 back-propagation paper uses this name.
A number fed into a model. The learner's two inputs are the holes in a card: 1 if punched, 0 if not.
One number for how wrong a model is on some examples. The learner's is the mean squared miss in hours. Training tries to make it small.
A common loss: square each miss, then average them. Big misses count extra. One neuron's loss of 9 is four misses of 3 hours each.
Another name for the loss, used in 3Blue1Brown's series.
For each dial, which way the loss would move if that dial turned a little, and how steeply.
Training by small steps: find each dial's gradient, turn every dial a little in the direction that lowers the loss, and repeat.
How big each gradient descent step is: every dial turns by its gradient times the learning rate. The learner's STRIDE knob.
A plan that changes the learning rate during training, usually lowering it as training goes on.
One pass through every training example. The learner takes one gradient descent step per epoch: one lesson through the four cards.
The method that finds every weight's gradient in one backward sweep, passing each neuron's share of the blame for the miss back through the layers.
To step past the lowest point and land on the far side. A learning rate that's too big overshoots.
When training's swings grow instead of settling, so the loss climbs and climbs. The learner diverged at 1.5.
To settle: more training steps stop lowering the loss because the weights have reached a low point.
Built only from multiplying by fixed numbers and adding. A weighted sum plus a bias is linear, and stacking linear steps stays linear.
Anything that isn't linear, like a sigmoid. Non-linear activations are what let layers of neurons learn shapes one neuron can't.
Short for exclusive or: yes when exactly one of two things is true. The mirror cards follow it, and one neuron can't learn it.
What a computer stores when a number grows too big to hold, printed as inf or Infinity. Sums with it soon give NaN.
Not a Number: what a computer gives for a sum with no meaningful answer, like infinity minus infinity. Once a weight is NaN, training can't recover.
Gradients so large that each training step throws the weights far off. Google's course says lowering the learning rate can help prevent them.
Gradient descent that takes each step on a small random group of examples instead of all of them: rougher steps, but much cheaper ones.
A small group of training examples used for one step of stochastic gradient descent.
A group of training examples processed together before one update of the weights.
An early, simpler kind of neural model. The 1986 back-propagation paper contrasts its own method with the perceptron's learning procedure.
One complete training job: a model, its data and its settings, trained from start to finish, often for hours or days.
Training an already-trained model a little more on your own examples. Season 8 covers it.
A running record of what a program did, usually one line per event.
A document that mixes runnable code with its results, popular for trying out models. Jupyter is the best-known kind.
One dot of a digital image. A 28 by 28 image has 784.
A free maths education channel and website that explains ideas with animation. Its Neural networks series is a common first introduction.
A guide from Google Research and Harvard authors on tuning deep learning training, including the learning rate and its schedule.
A clock with a mirror-image face whose hands turn the other way, so it reads correctly in a mirror. Also called a barber's clock.
A card that carries information as holes. The learner reads two possible holes on each card.
The nut under a pendulum's weight. Turning it lengthens or shortens the pendulum, so the clock runs slower or faster.

atWork: If your team trains or fine-tunes models, open the loss curve of a recent training run and read it the way Magda read her tape: a steady fall, a slow crawl, or swings that grow. Then find out what happens when a run's loss spikes or turns to NaN. Does anything alert a person, or does the job keep running, computing nothing? Where is the learning rate set, and is it fixed or on a schedule? Is a copy of the weights saved regularly, so a run that blows up can restart from before the blow-up? The first knobs to check after a spike are the learning rate (lower it) and the data the run was reading at that step: a missing value, or an example a thousand times bigger than the rest, can throw one huge step. If nobody on your team trains models, try it in a tutorial code notebook: train a small network, multiply its learning rate by ten until the loss blows up, and write down the first step where it does.

recall.prompt: Your team's overnight training run looked healthy until 3 AM. Then the loss jumped from 0.4 to 380, then to 90,000, and since 3:20 every log line has printed nan. A teammate wants to add more layers and let it run another night. What do you say, and what do you check first?

keyIdeas.idea: Jumps that grow point at steps that overshoot: the learning rate is probably too big
Lower the rate and restart from a saved copy from before the blow-up, not from the broken weights
More layers or more time won't fix a step that's too big
Look at the data around 3 AM for bad values, and watch the curve on the restarted run

recall.model: Don't add layers or let it go another night. Jumps that grow, 0.4 to 380 to 90,000, then nan, are the signature of steps that overshoot: the learning rate is too big for where the weights got to, or a bad batch of data threw one huge step. More layers won't fix the step size, and more time only lets the numbers grow. I'd lower the learning rate and restart from the last saved copy of the weights from before 3 AM, never from the broken ones, and look at the data it was reading around 3 AM for missing values or examples far bigger than the rest. Then I'd watch the loss curve on the restarted run, and add an alert so the next nan stops the job instead of letting it compute nothing all night.

recall.prompt: With the back row cut out, the learner settled on 6:00 for every card, a loss of 9.00. Why couldn't one neuron do better?
options: The knob at 0.1 was too small for it to finish learning
Its answer is a weighted sum, so two holes can't cancel out
Three dials can only store three different answers
It overfitted the four cards it learned from
recall.why: One neuron's answer is a weighted sum plus a bias, so each hole always moves the answer the same way by the same amount. The mirror cards need two holes to cancel, the XOR pattern. Its best compromise is 6 everywhere, a loss of 9, at any learning rate. A hidden layer with non-linear switches fixes it.

recall.prompt: The owner of a bakery chain asks how your demand forecast learns when nobody wrote its rules. Explain it in four or five plain sentences, no maths.

keyIdeas.idea: It has many adjustable dials (weights) between the inputs and the answer
One number, the loss, scores how wrong it is on past examples
Every dial is nudged a little in the direction that makes that number smaller
That is repeated over the examples many times, with the blame passed back to every dial

recall.model: It starts with thousands of dials set at random between what it's given, like the day of the week and the weather, and the number it predicts. We show it past days where we know how many loaves really sold and score how wrong its predictions were with one number. Then, working backwards from the prediction to share out the blame, we work out which way to turn every dial to make that number smaller, and turn each one a little. We repeat that over all the past days, many times, until the score stops improving. Finally we test it on recent weeks it never learned from, because doing well on the past isn't the same as predicting well.

recall.prompt: At 1.5, clock 4 read 3.15, then 3.34, 1.27, 25.14 and -49.53 hours. What is happening?
options: It's searching, and will settle once it finds the right time
The back row's switches have broken and are firing at random
Each turn overshoots by more than the last: the steps are too big
The reader is taking the four cards in the wrong order
recall.why: Swings to alternate sides that grow every lesson are divergence. Each turn lands further up the far side, where the slope is steeper, so the next turn is bigger still. More lessons make it worse; a smaller learning rate, from sensible dials, fixes it.

recall.prompt: What is one epoch for the learner?
options: One turn of a single dial
One stop on the STRIDE knob
One neuron in the back row
One pass through all four cards
recall.why: An epoch is one pass through every training example. The learner reads all four cards, then turns all 17 dials once: one gradient descent step per epoch. Google's course notes that training typically needs many epochs.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The learner is on Anselm's big lesson now: every rack in the cabinet, 3,124 dials, learning to read the time from 400 photographs of real clock faces. My apprentice, Pim, started it at 1.5 on the first night and it hit NaN by lesson 40, so he fitted a finer knob and set it to 0.0001, to be safe. Two weeks later the loss has gone from 52.0 to 51.3, and Pim wants to wire in the spare racks because, he says, the learner just isn't clever enough.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What is Pim's tape telling him, and what would you have him do first?

keyIdeas.idea: 0.0001 is far too small: the loss is falling, just very slowly
Reset and give a few rates between 0.0001 and 1.5 a short trial from the same dials; keep the largest whose loss falls steadily
More racks won't fix the step size
Hold back some photographs to check it on clocks it never learned from

coldCase.model: The tape isn't saying the learner is too small. It's saying the steps are tiny: 52.0 to 51.3 in two weeks is the slow crawl of a learning rate far too low, the opposite end from 1.5's blow-up. The right size is somewhere in between. I'd reset the dials and give a few rates a short trial each from the same starting dials, say 0.001, 0.01 and 0.1, and keep the largest one whose loss falls steadily without swinging. Only if the loss then flattens out at a high value with a good learning rate is it worth wiring in more racks, because more dials won't fix the step size. And I'd hold back some of the photographs: a low loss on the 400 it learns from doesn't prove it can read a clock it has never seen.

sources.title: 3Blue1Brown, Neural networks series, the gradient descent lesson (784 inputs, two hidden layers of 16 neurons, 10 outputs, 13,002 weights and biases; the cost adds up the squares of the differences, averaged over tens of thousands of training examples; learning means changing the weights and biases to minimize a cost function; compute this gradient direction, take a step downhill, and repeat; steps proportional to the slope keep you from overshooting)

3Blue1Brown, Neural networks series, the backpropagation lesson: What is backpropagation really doing? (an algorithm for computing that negative gradient; nudges passed to the layer before in proportion to the weights; mini-batches and stochastic gradient descent)

Google Machine Learning Crash Course: Linear regression, hyperparameters (the model multiplies the gradient by the learning rate; 2.5 times 0.01 is 0.025; too low takes a long time to converge, too high never converges but bounces around; an epoch is processing every example once; training typically requires many epochs)
Google Machine Learning Crash Course: Linear regression, gradient descent (move the weight and bias values a small amount in the direction that reduces loss, and repeat)
Google Machine Learning Crash Course: Linear regression, loss (loss is a numerical metric that describes how wrong a model's predictions are; mean squared error)

Google Machine Learning Crash Course: Neural networks, nodes and hidden layers (a hidden neuron takes the sum of each input times a unique weight, plus the bias; linear calculations on linear calculations stay linear)
Google Machine Learning Crash Course: Neural networks, activation functions (linear operations performed on linear operations are still linear; the sigmoid gives a value between 0 and 1)
Google Machine Learning Crash Course: Neural networks, training using backpropagation (exploding gradients; lowering the learning rate can help prevent them)

Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, Learning representations by back-propagating errors, Nature 323, 533 to 536 (1986): a procedure that repeatedly adjusts the weights to minimize the difference between actual and desired output; hidden units come to represent important features; contrasted with the perceptron-convergence procedure

Godbole, Dahl, Gilmer, Shallue and Nado, Deep Learning Tuning Playbook (Google Research and Harvard): different learning rates work best at different times during the optimization process, so some non-constant schedule matters
